newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Letter bombs only latest U.N. security scare.
newsitem.headline: Letter bombs only latest U.N. security scare.

text.p: The discovery of two letter bombs at the United Nations on Monday was only the latest security scare to plague the world body since it moved into its New York headquarters more than 45 years ago.
Previous incidents included an abortive bazooka attack, the planting of explosives in and around the U.N. complex and a feared kamikaze air strike.
The letter bombs, made harmless by the New York police bomb squad, were intended for the U.N. bureau of the Saudi-owned newspaper Al-Hayat.
Like a number of similar devices received at Al-Hayat's Washington bureau earlier this month, they were mailed from Egypt, according to U.N. sources.
One of several similar letter bombs exploded at Al-Hayat's London offices on Monday, wounding two security guards.
The bazooka attack entered U.N. folklore in December 1964 when Cuban revolutionary leader Che Guevara was addressing the General Assembly.
Anti-Castro groups signalled their displeasure by firing a rocket across the East River toward the 38-story United Nations. But it plopped harmlessly into the water and no damage was caused.

In August, 1966 five sticks of dynamite were discovered under a bench in the U.N. Meditation Room -- a sparsely-furnished chamber set aside for quiet contemplation. That was believed to be the first -- but not the last -- time a live device was found in or around the United Nations.

In March 1971, 16 anti-Castro Cuban students broke away from a U.N. guided tour and chained themselves to seats in the empty Security Council chamber. After they rejected an offer by U.N. security to leave peacefully, they were removed and turned over to New York police.

In October 1979 a man in a rented light plane caused the first-ever evacuation of the United Nations when he buzzed the area for about three hours, raising fears he intended crashing into the building.
Security officials were particularly edgy since Pope John Paul II had visited the United Nations only a few days earlier and Cuban President Fidel Castro was due to arrive soon afterwards.

When the pilot was arrested on landing at La Guardia airport he was found to be an Ohio-born resident of Australia disgruntled over his treatment by a New York publishing firm. Its offices, a few blocks from the United Nations, were the intended target of his buzzing.

A particularly messy, but non-lethal, incident occurred in the Security Council chamber in April 1980 when two demonstrators who obtained press passes ostensibly to cover a debate for a revolutionary publication dumped cans of red paint over then-Soviet ambassador Oleg Troyanovsky and deputy U.S. representative William Vanden Heuvel.
"Better red than dead," Troyanovsky joked later, though his American colleague claimed authorship of the quip.
In May, 1981, one visitor on a U.N.-guided tour stabbed and wounded another near the U.N. gift shop, for no apparent reason. The assailant was turned over to police.
In April 1992, the daughter of a Nobel Prize-winning physicist doused herself with gasoline and threatened to set herself on fire in a protest against taxes and war.
Holding a cigarette lighter in each hand, she sat in a locked van outside the U.N. secretariat building for 23 hours before surrendering to police and being taken to hospital for observation.
